A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same adaptive conformal weighting research, despite the AUKT-to-AdaConG renaming and broader framing. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-100 distillation, gridworld reinforcement learning, and SullyChen steering experiments in Tables 1–4 and Figure 3.

after.justification: v3 reports retained and revised experiments, plus original semi-supervised classification results, hyperparameter studies, and computational-cost measurements.

M1.justification: The conformal weighting core remains, but v3 Section 3.2.2 adds a semi-supervised procedure that calibrates on weakly augmented labeled data and weights pseudo-label consistency losses. Distillation switches from binary gating to exponential weighting, retaining binary gating as an alternative. The reinforcement-learning soft and hard variants primarily undergo renaming.

E1.justification: v3 adds semi-supervised classification on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and STL-10, substantially extending task and dataset coverage. It removes v1's milder CIFAR-100 corruption scenario, with standard deviation 0.03 on 30% of images, while retaining the stronger corruption scenario. Gridworld and SullyChen coverage remains.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's KD, FitNet, PKT, and FT homogeneous-distillation comparators, v3 Table 1 evaluates LS-KD, EA-KD, PTLoss, MSP, entropy, and MC dropout. The new SSL comparison evaluates UDA, FixMatch, and FlexMatch. Reinforcement-learning and driving comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported distillation batch size changes from 64 to 128. Heterogeneous experiments use stronger corruption and omit the ResNet32x4–MobileNet-V2 pairing. New SSL protocols introduce nine dataset/label-budget combinations, specified WRN backbones, and 51,200 training iterations. Sensitivity sweeps and runtime comparisons add further evaluation procedures.

E4.justification: v3 adds alpha and temperature sensitivity studies for distillation and SSL, steering alpha sensitivity, and prediction-set-size analysis in Figures 4–8 and 11. Table 6 adds computational-cost comparisons, while Table 5 examines the retained hard weighting against the new soft default. These substantially extend v1's analyses, although its two-corruption-level comparison is removed.

E5.justification: v1 provides distillation point estimates without a run count; v3 specifies four repeated runs and reports means and standard deviations in distillation Tables 1 and 4 and SSL Table 2. The ten-seed reinforcement-learning protocol is retained. This establishes expanded uncertainty reporting, without establishing an increase from a specified earlier distillation run count.

E6.justification: For ResNet110–ResNet20, baseline/augmented KD accuracy changes from 65.96/67.47% in v1 Table 2 to 57.23/66.53% in v3 Table 1, alongside changed weighting and batch size; these are replaced results rather than direct performance gains. New SSL results include FixMatch improving from 64.18% to 70.16% on CIFAR-10 with 40 labels. Driving Table 3 values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 changes the classification nonconformity expression from one minus predicted-class probability to one minus true-class probability. The appendix's gradient and MSE stationary-point argument is otherwise retained. However, v3 Equation 8 introduces an inconsistent derivative with respect to pretrained output fp, where v1 Equation 6 correctly differentiated the student output.

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from teacher–student knowledge transfer under unreliable teachers to guidance across supervised, semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning. v3 additionally claims the first framework embedding split conformal prediction into training across these settings. The useful-dark-knowledge claim and sixfold gridworld reward finding are retained.

C2.justification: v3 replaces v1's fixed-teacher and multi-teacher future-work discussion with limitations concerning exchangeability and target-domain calibration, explicitly distinguishing its uncertainty signal from strict coverage guarantees. Appendix A.2 now identifies the analysis as intuitive rather than a formal proof. New interpretations explain alpha/temperature tradeoffs and pseudo-label error propagation.

D1.justification: v3 documents the new SSL training recipe, including architectures, iteration budget, optimizer, learning rate, and regularization, and specifies ten forward passes for the MC-dropout cost comparison. Most existing hardware and training details remain. Reproducibility also loses some detail: v1's explicit unit driving-loss coefficients and MSE specification are replaced by a citation in v3 Appendix A.6.1.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from teacher–student transfer toward learning with diverse guidance signals, with direct contrasts against heuristic uncertainty weighting. New references include EA-KD, PTLoss, FixMatch, FlexMatch, and pseudo-label-noise research. Some earlier discussions and citations, including thermal transfer and LLM domain-adaptation examples, disappear.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten around AdaConG and multi-domain guidance. The separate problem definition is incorporated into the supervised-learning formulation, uncertainty-related discussion moves into the introduction, and method and appendix organization are substantially revised.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, Figures 1–2 are redrawn around multiple guidance sources, and Figure 3 changes from a two-by-two arrangement to a horizontal row with revised legends. Tables are expanded or restructured, and sensitivity plots and runtime tables are added. Environment diagrams and driving examples are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central uncertainty-weighting idea. Compared with v1's conventional distillation comparators and point estimates, it adds direct uncertainty-aware comparisons, run variability, sensitivity studies, and measured computational costs, making effectiveness and tradeoffs more assessable. SSL experiments test a substantively different guidance source, while the proof and coverage qualifications improve claim calibration. Benefits outweigh the introduced derivative inconsistency, reduced driving-loss detail, and an overbroad Table 1 superiority claim that its mixed baseline rankings do not fully support.
